Description: Listening: Can recognize familiar single words or fixed phrases in a teacher's oral description and respond by pointing to or naming the matching image. Speaking: Can produce single words or fixed phrases to label a familiar object when prompted.
Example: Shown a photo of a red bicycle, the student points to it when the teacher says "red bike," and says "red bike" back when asked "What is this?"

Description: Can decode an unfamiliar simple word or short adjective-noun phrase (e.g. sounding out "big," "red," "hat") using known letter-sound patterns, and match it to the object or image it describes, with visual support.
Example: Given the printed word "cat" (never drilled as a sight word) next to pictures of a cat and a dog, the student sounds out /k/-/a/-/t/ and points to the cat.

Description: Can spell a simple word from sound using known letter-sound patterns (e.g. "hat," "big," "red") to describe a familiar object, using a memorized adjective-noun frame ("big ___").
Example: Shown a picture of a big dog and given the frame "big ___," the student sounds out and writes "dog," rather than copying it from a word list.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken sequence of events (3–4 steps) supported by non-verbal cues and identify or point to the correct order using single words. Speaking: Can retell a very short personal event using isolated words or short fixed phrases and gesture, with listener support.
Example: The teacher tells a 3-step story (woke up, ate breakfast, went to school) with gestures and pictures; the student points to the pictures in order, then retells it: "woke up… eat… school," using gestures.

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple action/sequence words (e.g. "ran," "sat," "left") using known letter-sound patterns and match them to the correct step of a short personal event shown in sequence, with visual support.
Example: Given three photos of a birthday party in mixed-up order and the unfamiliar word "blew" beside one, the student sounds it out and matches it to the photo of blowing out candles.

Description: Can spell simple action/sequence words from sound using known letter-sound patterns to name events in a short personal story, using memorized time-order chunks ("first," "then") as the frame around the spelled word.
Example: Looking at 3 photos of their weekend (park, lunch, home), the student writes "first" under photo 1 and spells "park" from sound to caption it.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a simple spoken cause-effect pair supported by visuals/demonstration and match cause to effect by pointing or selecting. Speaking: Can produce a single-word or fixed-phrase response naming a cause or effect when prompted ("Why?" → one word/phrase answer).
Example: Shown a picture of rain and a person opening an umbrella, the teacher asks "Why?" and the student says "rain."

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple cause/effect words (e.g. "wet," "hot," "fell") using known letter-sound patterns and match a cause to its effect, with visual support.
Example: Given a picture of ice cream melting in the sun and the unfamiliar word "hot" printed nearby, the student sounds it out and matches it to the melting/effect side of the pair.

Description: Can spell simple cause/effect words from sound using known letter-sound patterns to name a cause or effect in a simple process, using a memorized connector chunk ("because," "so") as the frame around the spelled word.
Example: Given the frame "___, so I put on a coat" and a picture of someone bundled up outside, the student spells "cold" into the frame from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a simple spoken instruction supported by demonstration or visuals and carry out or point to the correct step (1–2 step commands). Speaking: Can produce a single-word or fixed-phrase instruction to direct a partner's simple physical action, with gesture support.
Example: The teacher says "Stand up" with a gesture; the student stands, then later tells a partner "Sit down," using the same fixed phrase.

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple action words (e.g. "cut," "mix," "stop") using known letter-sound patterns and match them to the correct step of a simple instruction sequence, with visual support.
Example: Given step pictures for washing hands and the unfamiliar word "turn" beside one step, the student sounds it out and points to the matching step (turning on the tap).

Description: Can spell simple action words from sound using known letter-sound patterns to name the steps of a simple procedure, using memorized imperative-form chunks ("do this, then this") as the frame around the spelled word.
Example: Given picture steps for making a sandwich, the student spells "cut" from sound under the first step.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a simple spoken opinion supported by visuals or demonstration and identify whether it is positive or negative (point/select "good"/"not good"). Speaking: Can produce a single-word or fixed-phrase opinion in response to a prompt ("How is it?" → "good"/"bad").
Example: Shown a picture of spoiled milk, the teacher says "This is bad" with a frown; the student points to "not good," then says "bad" when asked "How is it?"

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple evaluative words (e.g. "good," "bad," "fun") using known letter-sound patterns and identify whether they express a positive or negative reaction, with visual support.
Example: Given a photo of a messy room and the unfamiliar word "bad" printed beside it, the student sounds it out and selects the frowning-face rating.

Description: Can spell simple evaluative words from sound using known letter-sound patterns to express a like/dislike or good/bad judgment, using a memorized evaluative frame ("I like ___, it's ___") around the spelled word.
Example: Given a photo of ice cream, the student spells "good" from sound to complete "I like ice cream, it's good."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a simple spoken preference supported by visuals/demonstration and identify what is being preferred (point/select). Speaking: Can produce a single-word or fixed-phrase preference in response to a prompt ("Which one?" → naming one item).
Example: Shown a red shirt and a blue shirt, the teacher asks "Which one?"; the student points to the red shirt and says "red."

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple stance words (e.g. "this," "that," "yes") using known letter-sound patterns and identify which option is being preferred, with visual support.
Example: Given two food pictures and the unfamiliar word "that" printed under one, the student sounds it out and points to the corresponding picture as the chosen option.

Description: Can spell a simple preferred item's name from sound using known letter-sound patterns to state a simple position, using the memorized frame ("I want ___") around the spelled word.
Example: Given two drink pictures, the student spells "juice" from sound to complete "I want juice."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a simple spoken transactional exchange (e.g., ordering, buying) supported by visuals/realia and identify what is being requested or offered (point/select). Speaking: Can produce a single-word or fixed-phrase request in a simple transactional exchange, with gesture support.
Example: Role-playing a snack stand with real objects, the teacher asks "What do you want?"; the student points to an apple and says "Apple, please."

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple transactional words (e.g. item names, numbers) using known letter-sound patterns and identify what is being requested or offered in a simple transactional exchange (e.g., ordering, buying), with visual support.
Example: Given a simple order form with a sandwich picture and the unfamiliar word "two" printed beside it, the student sounds out "two" and matches it to two sandwiches.

Description: Can spell simple item names or numbers from sound using known letter-sound patterns to complete a simple transactional exchange in writing, using memorized frames ("one ___, please") around the spelled word.
Example: Given a picture of juice, the student spells "juice" from sound to complete "One juice, please."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a simple spoken social exchange (greeting, introduction) supported by visuals/gesture and identify the social move being made (point/select "hello"/"goodbye"/"thank you"). Speaking: Can produce a single-word or fixed-phrase social exchange (greeting, thanks, farewell) with gesture support.
Example: Meeting someone new, the teacher waves and says "Hi, I'm Sam"; the student waves and says "Hi" (or their own name) when prompted.

Description: Can decode unfamiliar simple social words/phrases (e.g. "hi," "bye," "thanks") using known letter-sound patterns and identify the social move being made (greeting, thanks, farewell), with visual support.
Example: Given a picture of two people waving goodbye and the unfamiliar word "bye" printed beside it, the student sounds it out and identifies it as the correct social move.

Description: Can spell simple social words from sound using known letter-sound patterns for a simple social exchange in writing (greeting, thanks, simple wish), using memorized functional frames around the spelled word.
Example: Given a picture of someone leaving and the frame "___, see you!", the student spells "bye" from sound to complete it.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken description using a fixed frame ("It is ___.") supported by visuals, and identify the described object among 2–3 choices. Speaking: Can produce one sentence describing a familiar object using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Shown a picture of a ball and asked "What is it like?", the student, prompted, says "It is round."

Description: Can read one short sentence using the fixed frame ("It is ___.") describing a familiar object, decoding the open-slot word using known letter-sound patterns to identify the matching image, with visual support.
Example: Given "It is small." next to pictures of a mouse and an elephant, the student decodes "small" and points to the mouse.

Description: Can spell the open-slot word in the fixed frame ("It is ___.") from sound to describe a familiar object, prompted by a picture.
Example: Shown a cup of hot coffee and given "It is ___.", the student spells "hot" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken sentence narrating a single past action using a fixed frame ("I ___-ed.") supported by visuals, and identify the matching picture. Speaking: Can produce one sentence narrating a single past action using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Shown a picture of a child kicking a ball and asked "What did you do?", the student, prompted, says "I played."

Description: Can read one short sentence using the fixed frame ("I ___-ed.") narrating a single past action, decoding the open-slot word to identify the matching image, with visual support.
Example: Given "I walked." next to pictures of walking and running, the student decodes "walked" and points to the walking picture.

Description: Can spell the open-slot verb in the fixed frame ("I ___-ed.") from sound to narrate a single past action, prompted by a picture.
Example: Shown a picture of someone cooking and given "I ___-ed.", the student spells "cooked" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken cause-effect sentence using a fixed frame ("It's [effect] because it's ___.") supported by visuals, and identify the matching cause. Speaking: Can produce one cause-effect sentence using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Shown a picture of a puddle and asked "Why is it wet?", the student, prompted, says "It's wet because it's rainy."

Description: Can read one short cause-effect sentence using the fixed frame, decoding the open-slot reason word to identify the matching image, with visual support.
Example: Given "It's wet because it's rainy." next to a sunny-day and a rainy-day picture, the student decodes "rainy" and points to the rainy picture.

Description: Can spell the open-slot reason word in the fixed cause-effect frame from sound, prompted by a picture.
Example: Shown a rainy-day picture and given "It's wet because it's ___.", the student spells "rainy" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken instruction using a fixed frame ("First, ___.") supported by visuals/demonstration, and identify or carry out the correct first step. Speaking: Can give one instruction using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Shown step pictures for making a sandwich and asked "What's first?", the student, prompted, says "First, cut."

Description: Can read one short instruction using the fixed frame, decoding the open-slot action word to identify the matching first step, with visual support.
Example: Given "First, mix." next to pictures of mixing and pouring, the student decodes "mix" and points to the mixing picture.

Description: Can spell the open-slot action word in the fixed instruction frame from sound, prompted by a picture of the first step.
Example: Shown a picture of stirring a bowl and given "First, ___.", the student spells "stir" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken opinion-with-reason sentence using a fixed frame supported by visuals, and identify the item and its reason. Speaking: Can give one opinion-with-reason sentence using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Shown a picture of a sports car and asked "How is it?", the student, prompted, says "It's good because it's fast."

Description: Can read one short opinion-with-reason sentence using the fixed frame, decoding the open-slot reason word to identify the matching item, with visual support.
Example: Given "It's good because it's fast." next to a bicycle and a sports car, the student decodes "fast" and points to the car.

Description: Can spell the open-slot reason word in the fixed opinion frame from sound, prompted by a picture.
Example: Shown a picture of a sports car and given "It's good because it's ___.", the student spells "fast" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken preference-with-reason sentence using a fixed frame supported by visuals, and identify the preferred option and its reason. Speaking: Can state one preference-with-reason sentence using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Shown a big cookie and a small cookie and asked "Which one, and why?", the student, prompted, says "I want this one because it's bigger."

Description: Can read one short preference-with-reason sentence using the fixed frame, decoding the open-slot reason word to identify the matching option, with visual support.
Example: Given "I want this one because it's bigger." next to a big cookie and a small cookie, the student decodes "bigger" and points to the big cookie.

Description: Can spell the open-slot reason word in the fixed preference frame from sound, prompted by two pictures.
Example: Shown a big cookie and given "I want this one because it's ___.", the student spells "bigger" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken request using a fixed frame ("I want one ___, please.") supported by visuals/realia, and identify what is being requested. Speaking: Can make one request using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Role-playing a snack stand and asked "What do you want?", the student, prompted, says "I want one apple, please."

Description: Can read one short request sentence using the fixed frame, decoding the open-slot item word to identify what's being requested, with visual support.
Example: Given "I want one juice, please." next to pictures of juice and milk, the student decodes "juice" and points to the juice.

Description: Can spell the open-slot item word in the fixed request frame from sound, prompted by a picture.
Example: Shown a picture of juice and given "I want one ___, please.", the student spells "juice" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken social sentence using a fixed frame ("Thank you for the ___.") supported by visuals/gesture, and identify what's being thanked for. Speaking: Can produce one social sentence using the memorized frame with one open slot, prompted by the teacher.
Example: Handed a gift and prompted, the student says "Thank you for the gift."

Description: Can read one short social sentence using the fixed frame, decoding the open-slot word to identify what's being thanked for, with visual support.
Example: Given "Thank you for the card." next to pictures of a card and a gift box, the student decodes "card" and points to the card.

Description: Can spell the open-slot word in the fixed thank-you frame from sound, prompted by a picture.
Example: Shown a picture of a card and given "Thank you for the ___.", the student spells "card" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken description using a two-slot frame ("It is ___ and ___.") and identify the described object among a small set of choices, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can describe a familiar object using the memorized frame with two open slots, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Given a reference card showing "It is ___ and ___." and shown a big red umbrella, the student says "It is big and red."

Description: Can read one short sentence using the two-slot frame describing a familiar object, decoding both open-slot words using known letter-sound patterns to identify the matching image.
Example: Given "It is big and red." next to a small blue umbrella and a big red umbrella, the student decodes both words and points to the big red umbrella.

Description: Can spell both open-slot words in the two-slot frame from sound to describe a familiar object.
Example: Shown a big red umbrella and given "It is ___ and ___.", the student spells "big" and "red" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken sentence narrating two sequential past actions using a two-slot frame and identify the matching picture pair, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can narrate two sequential past actions using the memorized frame with two open slots, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Shown two pictures in order (cooking, then cleaning) and a reference card, the student says "I cooked and cleaned."

Description: Can read one short sentence using the two-slot frame narrating two sequential past actions, decoding both open-slot words to identify the matching picture pair.
Example: Given "I cooked and cleaned." next to two picture-pair options, the student decodes both words and points to the cooking-then-cleaning pair.

Description: Can spell both open-slot verbs in the two-slot past-tense frame from sound to narrate two sequential actions.
Example: Shown pictures of cooking then cleaning and given "I ___-ed and ___-ed.", the student spells "cooked" and "cleaned" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken cause-effect sentence with two coordinated reasons using a two-slot frame and identify the matching cause, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can give a cause-effect sentence with two coordinated reasons using the memorized frame, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Shown a picture of a storm and a reference card, the student says "It's wet because it's rainy and windy."

Description: Can read one short cause-effect sentence with two coordinated reasons using the frame, decoding both open-slot words to identify the matching cause.
Example: Given "It's wet because it's rainy and windy." next to a calm sunny picture and a stormy picture, the student decodes both words and points to the stormy picture.

Description: Can spell both open-slot reason words in the cause-effect frame from sound.
Example: Shown a stormy picture and given "It's wet because it's ___ and ___.", the student spells "rainy" and "windy" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short two-step spoken instruction using a two-slot frame ("First, ___. Then, ___.") and identify or carry out both steps in order, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can give a two-step instruction using the memorized frame with two open slots, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Shown step pictures for making a sandwich and a reference card, the student says "First, cut. Then, mix."

Description: Can read a short two-step instruction using the frame, decoding both open-slot action words to identify the matching steps in order.
Example: Given "First, cut. Then, mix." next to three step pictures, the student decodes both words and points to them in order.

Description: Can spell both open-slot action words in the two-step instruction frame from sound.
Example: Shown step pictures for making a sandwich and given "First, ___. Then, ___.", the student spells "cut" and "mix" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken opinion sentence with two coordinated reasons using a two-slot frame and identify the item and its reasons, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can give an opinion with two coordinated reasons using the memorized frame, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Shown a picture of a sports car and a reference card, the student says "It's good because it's fast and cheap."

Description: Can read one short opinion sentence with two coordinated reasons using the frame, decoding both open-slot words to identify the matching item.
Example: Given "It's good because it's fast and cheap." next to a luxury car and a compact car, the student decodes both words and points to the compact car.

Description: Can spell both open-slot reason words in the opinion frame from sound.
Example: Shown a compact car and given "It's good because it's ___ and ___.", the student spells "fast" and "cheap" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken preference sentence with two coordinated reasons using a two-slot frame and identify the preferred option and its reasons, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can state a preference with two coordinated reasons using the memorized frame, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Shown a big cookie and a small cookie and a reference card, the student says "I want this one because it's bigger and cheaper."

Description: Can read one short preference sentence with two coordinated reasons using the frame, decoding both open-slot words to identify the matching option.
Example: Given "I want this one because it's bigger and cheaper." next to a big cookie and a small cookie, the student decodes both words and points to the big cookie.

Description: Can spell both open-slot reason words in the preference frame from sound.
Example: Shown a big cookie and given "I want this one because it's ___ and ___.", the student spells "bigger" and "cheaper" from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken request for two items using a two-slot frame and identify what is being requested, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can request two items using the memorized frame with two open slots, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Role-playing a snack stand with a reference card, the student says "I want juice and a sandwich, please."

Description: Can read one short request sentence for two items using the frame, decoding both open-slot words to identify what's being requested.
Example: Given "I want juice and a sandwich, please." next to pictures of several items, the student decodes both words and points to the juice and sandwich.

Description: Can spell both open-slot item words in the request frame from sound.
Example: Shown pictures of juice and a sandwich and given "I want ___ and ___, please.", the student spells both words from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to one short spoken thank-you sentence for two items using a two-slot frame and identify what's being thanked for, with a model available for reference. Speaking: Can thank someone for two things using the memorized frame with two open slots, with a model available rather than being prompted step-by-step.
Example: Handed a card and a gift and given a reference card, the student says "Thank you for the card and the gift."

Description: Can read one short thank-you sentence for two items using the frame, decoding both open-slot words to identify what's being thanked for.
Example: Given "Thank you for the card and the gift." next to pictures of several items, the student decodes both words and points to the card and gift.

Description: Can spell both open-slot words in the thank-you frame from sound.
Example: Shown a card and a gift and given "Thank you for the ___ and the ___.", the student spells both words from sound.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken description of a familiar object, choosing their own connectors, and identify its features, one comparison, and the brief reason given for that comparison. Speaking: Can produce a short original description of a familiar object including one comparison and a brief reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Shown a laptop, the student says: "It's a laptop. It's small and light, lighter than my old one, because I need to carry it every day."

Description: Can read a short descriptive text about a familiar object and identify its features, one comparison, and the brief reason given for that comparison, decoding unfamiliar words as needed using known letter-sound patterns.
Example: Given "It's a laptop. It's small and light, lighter than my old one, because I need to carry it every day," the student identifies the object, the comparison, and the reason (carrying it daily).

Description: Can write a short original description of a familiar object including one comparison and a brief reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Shown a backpack, the student writes "It's a backpack. It's blue and big, bigger than my old bag, because I need room for my books."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken narration of a sequence of past events, choosing their own time connectors, and identify the order, one outcome, and the brief reason given for that outcome. Speaking: Can narrate a short original sequence of past events including one outcome and a brief reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Shown three photos of a rushed morning, the student says "First I woke up late. Then I got dressed fast. I still missed the bus because it left early that day."

Description: Can read a short narrative text and identify the sequence of events, one outcome, and the brief reason given for that outcome, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "First I woke up late. Then I got dressed fast. I still missed the bus because it left early that day," the student identifies the sequence and the reason the outcome happened.

Description: Can write a short original narrative recounting a sequence of past events with one outcome and a brief reason for it, choosing their own time connectors, working independently.
Example: Given three photos of cooking a meal, the student writes "First I chopped vegetables. Then I cooked them. Dinner was a little late because I chopped too slowly."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken explanation of a familiar process with two linked causes/steps, choosing their own connectors, and identify the causes, the outcome, and which cause the speaker considers more important. Speaking: Can explain a familiar two-cause process in a short original explanation, choosing their own connectors, and state which of the two causes matters more, working independently.
Example: Asked why their plant died, the student says "Plants need water and light. Mine got plenty of light, but I forgot to water it — that's really what killed it."

Description: Can read a short explanatory text and identify two linked causes/steps, the outcome, and which cause the writer treats as more important, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "Plants need water and light. Mine got plenty of light, but I forgot to water it — that's really what killed it," the student identifies both causes and which one the writer blames most.

Description: Can write a short original explanation of a familiar two-cause process, choosing their own connectors, and state which of the two causes matters more, working independently.
Example: Asked why their phone died, the student writes "Phones need charging and a good battery. Mine still has a good battery, but I keep forgetting to charge it — that's the real problem."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken set of instructions for a familiar task including one warning, choosing their own sequencing connectors, and identify the steps, the warning, and the brief reason given for it. Speaking: Can give a short original set of instructions for a familiar task including one warning and the reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Explaining how to cook pasta, the student says "First, boil water. Then add the pasta and stir it, because if you don't, it sticks to the pot."

Description: Can read a short set of instructions and identify the steps, the warning, and the brief reason given for it, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "First, boil water. Then add the pasta and stir it, because if you don't, it sticks to the pot," the student identifies the steps and the reason for the stirring warning.

Description: Can write a short original set of instructions for a familiar task including one warning and the reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Asked how to make toast, the student writes "First, put the bread in. Don't leave it too long, because it burns fast once it starts."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken evaluation of a familiar item using one criterion and one comparison, choosing their own connectors, and identify the criterion, the comparison, the verdict, and the brief reason for the criterion mattering. Speaking: Can evaluate a familiar item in a short original opinion using one criterion, one comparison, and a brief reason the criterion matters to them, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Asked about a nearby restaurant, the student says "This restaurant is good — it's fast, which matters because I only get a short lunch break. It's better than the one downtown."

Description: Can read a short opinion text and identify the criterion, the comparison, the overall verdict, and the brief reason given for why the criterion matters, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "This restaurant is good — it's fast, which matters because I only get a short lunch break. It's better than the one downtown," the student identifies the criterion, verdict, and the reason it matters to the writer.

Description: Can write a short original opinion about a familiar item using one criterion, one comparison, and a brief reason the criterion matters to them, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Asked about their phone, the student writes "My phone is great — it's reliable, which matters because I use it for work. It's better than my old one."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken position with one reason and one simple counterpoint, choosing their own connectors, and identify the position, its reason, the counterpoint, and the brief reason the counterpoint doesn't change the speaker's mind. Speaking: Can state a short original position with one reason and one simple counterpoint, briefly explaining why the counterpoint doesn't change their mind, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Asked how to get to work, the student says "I think we should walk. It's healthier. It does take longer, but that's fine with me because I like the extra time to think."

Description: Can read a short position text and identify the position, its reason, the acknowledged counterpoint, and the brief reason the counterpoint doesn't outweigh the position, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "I think we should walk. It's healthier. It does take longer, but that's fine with me because I like the extra time to think," the student identifies the position, reason, counterpoint, and why the writer isn't persuaded by it.

Description: Can write a short original position with one reason and one simple counterpoint, briefly explaining why the counterpoint doesn't change their mind, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Asked about working from home, the student writes "I like working from home. It's quieter. I do miss my coworkers, but I'm still more productive, so it's worth it."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken transactional exchange involving a simple problem, choosing their own connectors, and identify the problem, the proposed solution, and the brief reason the solution is acceptable. Speaking: Can handle a short original transactional exchange involving a simple problem, proposing a solution and briefly explaining why it's acceptable, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Told a size is unavailable, the student says "Do you have a medium instead? That's fine — I mostly wear it loose anyway, so it should still work."

Description: Can read a short transactional text and identify the problem, the proposed solution, and the brief reason given for accepting it, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "Do you have a medium instead? That's fine — I mostly wear it loose anyway, so it should still work," the student identifies the request, the substitute, and why it's acceptable.

Description: Can write a short original transactional message handling a simple problem, proposing a solution and briefly explaining why it's acceptable, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Told their delivery is late, the student writes "Could you check the status? I'd also be fine with a refund, since I already found the item somewhere else."

Description: Listening: Can listen to a short spoken social exchange involving a polite decline or topic change, choosing their own connectors, and identify the social move being made and the brief reason given for it. Speaking: Can carry out a short original social exchange involving a polite decline or topic change, giving a brief reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Invited to an event, the student says "Thanks for the invite, but I can't make it — I already have plans that night. Maybe next time?"

Description: Can read a short social text and identify the polite decline or topic change being made and the brief reason given for it, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given "Thanks for the invite, but I can't make it — I already have plans that night. Maybe next time?" the student identifies this as a decline and names the reason given.

Description: Can write a short original social message involving a polite decline or topic change, giving a brief reason for it, choosing their own connectors, working independently.
Example: Invited to a party they can't attend, the student writes "Thank you so much for inviting me, but I already have plans that weekend. I hope it goes really well!"

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken description of a familiar or semi-familiar place or object, summarize how it's organized, and identify one clearly evaluative word choice that signals the speaker's opinion even though the speaker never states the opinion directly (e.g. a positive or negative adjective standing in for "I like/dislike this"). Speaking: Can give an extended description, organizing details logically and including at least one clearly evaluative word choice that signals an opinion without stating it outright, working independently.
Example: Asked to describe their neighborhood, the student says: "My neighborhood is quiet and green. There are many trees and a small park nearby. The houses are old, but everyone keeps their garden nice." The word "nice" is a clear positive signal standing in for "I like it," and the student can point to that word when asked how they feel about the neighborhood.

Description: Can read an extended description, summarize how the writer organizes details, and identify at least one clearly evaluative word choice that signals the writer's attitude even though the writer never states the opinion directly, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a paragraph describing a neighborhood that says the houses are old but everyone "keeps their garden nice," the student summarizes the paragraph's organization and identifies "nice" as a clear positive signal of the writer's approval, even though the writer never writes "I like this neighborhood."

Description: Can write an extended description of a familiar or semi-familiar place or object, organizing details logically and including at least one detail that implies an opinion or attitude without stating it directly, working independently.
Example: Asked to describe their workplace, the student writes a paragraph covering its layout and atmosphere, choosing a detail (e.g., "everyone leaves their door open") that implies a friendly culture without writing "it's a friendly place."

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken narration of a personal event, summarize the sequence and why it mattered, and identify one clearly telling action or detail that signals how the speaker felt, even though the speaker never names the feeling directly. Speaking: Can narrate an extended account of a personal event, stating why it mattered and including at least one clearly telling action or detail that signals a feeling without naming it outright, working independently.
Example: Asked about a memorable trip, the student narrates a weekend away and says "I checked the return train time three times before we even left" -- a clearly repeated, countable action that signals nervousness or reluctance to leave, without the student ever saying "I didn't want to go home."

Description: Can read an extended narration, summarize the sequence of events and why they mattered, and identify at least one clearly telling action or detail that signals how someone felt, even though the feeling is never named directly, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a paragraph about a coworker's difficult commute that says they "checked the time every few minutes, then checked it again," the student summarizes what happened and identifies that repeated, countable action as a clear signal of anxiety, even though the word "anxious" never appears.

Description: Can write an extended narration of a personal event, stating why it mattered and including at least one detail that implies a feeling without naming it directly, working independently.
Example: Asked about their first week at a new job, the student writes a paragraph recounting it, including a detail (rehearsing what to say before a meeting) that implies nervousness without ever writing the word.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken explanation of a semi-familiar multi-step process, summarize how the steps or causes connect, and identify one clear signal word or phrase (e.g. "which happens more than you'd think," "unfortunately") that shows the speaker's frustration with a step, even though the frustration is never named directly. Speaking: Can explain a semi-familiar multi-step process, and include at least one clear signal word or phrase that shows frustration or preference about a step without stating it outright, working independently.
Example: Asked how their commute usually goes, the student explains the multi-step process and adds "and then, if the bus is late, which happens more than you'd think, I just walk" -- the phrase "more than you'd think" is a clear, recognizable signal of frustration with the bus's reliability, without the student saying "the bus is unreliable."

Description: Can read an extended explanation, summarize the steps or causes and how they connect, and identify at least one clear signal word or phrase that shows the writer's frustration or preference about a step, even though it is never named directly, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a paragraph explaining how a package gets delivered that says a step "usually, but not always, happens on time," the student summarizes the process and identifies "but not always" as a clear, recognizable signal of mild frustration with that step's reliability.

Description: Can write an extended explanation of a semi-familiar multi-step process, including at least one moment that implies a preference or frustration about a step without stating it directly, working independently.
Example: Asked how their team handles a request at work, the student writes a paragraph explaining the process and includes a phrase ("which takes longer than it probably should") that implies frustration without directly criticizing the process.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken set of instructions for a moderately complex task, including one flagged risk, summarize the steps, and identify one clear signal (repetition, "seriously," "make sure") that shows a step matters more than the others. Speaking: Can give an extended set of instructions for a moderately complex familiar task, flagging one risk and using a clear signal (repetition or an emphasis word) to show that one step matters more than the others, working independently.
Example: Asked how to set up their home wifi router, the student gives instructions and says "and don't forget to restart the modem, seriously, don't skip that" -- the repeated instruction and the word "seriously" are a clear, recognizable signal that this step is a common failure point.

Description: Can read an extended set of instructions, summarize the steps and the flagged risk, and identify at least one clear signal word or phrase (e.g. "make sure," "be careful here") that shows a step matters more than the others, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given instructions for jump-starting a car where one step includes the words "be very careful here," the student summarizes the steps and identifies that phrase as a clear signal that this step is riskier than the others, even without a separate warning label.

Description: Can write an extended set of instructions for a moderately complex familiar task, flagging one risk and implying, through emphasis or word choice, that one step matters more than the others, working independently.
Example: Asked how to use the office coffee machine, the student writes instructions and adds "make sure it's actually off before you leave" in a way that implies this is where people usually go wrong, without stating that outright.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken evaluation that weighs two criteria, summarize the criteria and verdict, and identify one clear hedging word or phrase (e.g. "for now," "so far") that signals a reservation about the verdict. Speaking: Can evaluate something using two criteria weighed against each other, and include at least one clear hedging word or phrase that signals a reservation about the verdict, working independently.
Example: Asked to evaluate their current job, the student weighs pay against work-life balance and adds "so overall it's good, for now" -- the phrase "for now" is a clear, recognizable hedge that signals a reservation about the future, without directly saying they're worried.

Description: Can read an extended evaluation, summarize the criteria and the overall verdict, and identify at least one clear hedging word or phrase that signals a reservation about the writer's own verdict, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a review weighing a phone plan's price against its coverage that ends with "solid choice, at least for now," the student summarizes the trade-off and verdict, and identifies "at least for now" as a clear, recognizable hedge signaling a reservation.

Description: Can write an extended evaluation using two criteria weighed against each other, including at least one moment that implies a reservation about the verdict without stating it directly, working independently.
Example: Asked to evaluate a nearby gym, the student weighs price against equipment quality and ends with "worth it, as long as it stays this way" -- implying an unstated worry about future price increases.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken argument with a claim, two reasons, and an addressed counterargument, summarize all three, and identify one clear hedging word or phrase (e.g. "I guess," "probably") that signals the speaker is less than fully certain. Speaking: Can construct an extended argument with a claim, two reasons, and an addressed counterargument, including at least one clear hedging word or phrase that signals partial uncertainty, working independently.
Example: Asked their opinion on remote work, the student argues for it, addresses the isolation counterpoint, and adds "though I guess it depends on the person" -- "I guess" is a clear, recognizable hedge that signals the argument isn't fully absolute, without directly walking it back.

Description: Can read an extended argument, summarize the claim, its two reasons, and the addressed counterargument, and identify at least one clear hedging word or phrase that signals the writer's partial uncertainty, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a paragraph arguing for a four-day work week that ends with "though results probably vary by industry," the student summarizes the claim and reasons, and identifies "probably vary" as a clear, recognizable hedge signaling the writer isn't fully certain the argument applies everywhere.

Description: Can write an extended argument with a claim, two reasons, and an addressed counterargument, including at least one moment that implies partial uncertainty without stating it directly, working independently.
Example: Asked their opinion on carpooling to work, the student argues for it, addresses the scheduling counterpoint, and ends with "at least, it's worked for me so far" -- implying an unstated awareness that it might not work for everyone.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken transactional message that states a purpose, gives detail, and requests an outcome, summarize all three, and identify one clear urgency signal within polite phrasing (e.g. "really appreciate," "as soon as possible") even though the word "urgent" is never used. Speaking: Can deliver an extended transactional message stating a purpose, giving detail, and requesting an outcome, using a clear urgency signal within polite phrasing without using the word "urgent" directly, working independently.
Example: Calling to reschedule an appointment, the student explains the conflict, gives their availability, and adds "if there's any way to fit me in sooner, I'd really appreciate it" -- "really appreciate" and "sooner" are clear, recognizable urgency signals, without the student saying "this is urgent."

Description: Can read an extended transactional message, summarize the purpose, the detail given, and the requested outcome, and identify at least one clear urgency signal within polite phrasing, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a message requesting a refund that says "I'd appreciate a response whenever you get a chance, though sooner would be great," the student summarizes the request and identifies "sooner would be great" as a clear, recognizable urgency signal within the polite wording.

Description: Can write an extended transactional message stating a purpose, giving detail, and requesting an outcome, using polite phrasing that implies urgency without stating it directly, working independently.
Example: Needing to reschedule a delivery, the student writes a message explaining the conflict and proposing a new time, phrasing the request as "if at all possible" in a way that implies real time pressure without stating a deadline outright.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken social message, summarize its tone and purpose, and identify one clear intensifying word (e.g. "honestly," "really," "genuinely") that signals a feeling that isn't named directly. Speaking: Can deliver an extended social message matching tone to the occasion, including at least one clear intensifying word that signals a feeling without naming it directly, working independently.
Example: Congratulating a coworker on a promotion, the student says "you've earned every bit of this, honestly" -- "honestly" is a clear, recognizable signal of genuine happiness for the person beyond simple politeness, without stating a feeling directly.

Description: Can read an extended social message, summarize its tone and purpose, and identify at least one clear intensifying word that signals a feeling that isn't named directly, decoding unfamiliar words as needed.
Example: Given a thank-you note that says "I genuinely don't know what I would have done without your help," the student summarizes what it's thanking the recipient for and identifies "genuinely" as a clear, recognizable signal of real relief, not just politeness.

Description: Can write an extended social message matching tone to the occasion, including at least one word choice that implies a feeling without naming it directly, working independently.
Example: Thanking a mentor for their help, the student writes "I don't think I would have gotten through that project without you" -- implying genuine gratitude and relief without writing "I am grateful" outright.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended spoken description and distinguish the speaker's stated facts from their clearly-signaled evaluative comments (e.g. "the real upside is," "what's nice about it is"). Speaking: Can deliver a fluent, integrated extended description that moves between features and their significance without a fixed template, explicitly explaining why at least one feature matters, and adjusting register or approach at least once in response to a specific listener reaction, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Describing a product to a friend deciding whether to buy it, the student says "It's not cheap, but it's built to last, and honestly, that's the real upside," clearly flagging "the real upside" as their own evaluation rather than a plain fact, then notices their friend still looks unconvinced and switches from general praise to one concrete comparison that speaks directly to the friend's stated budget.

Description: Can read an extended description and identify specific word choices that create a positive, negative, or neutral impression, separating explicitly stated description from clearly-signaled evaluative comments, and locate at least one place where the writer's language visibly shifts partway through (e.g. from confident claims to a hedge like "results may vary").
Example: Given a product description that opens with confident marketing language and grows more hedged in its final lines ("results may vary"), the student separates fact from clearly-signaled opinion throughout and locates the shift into hedged language at the end of the text.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated extended description that moves between features and their significance without a fixed template, explicitly explaining why at least one feature matters to a specified reader, and adjusting register or approach at least once to address a stated reader concern, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Asked to describe their apartment to a prospective roommate who mentioned caring most about quiet, the student writes an integrated description that opens broadly, then shifts specifically to noise and layout once that priority is on the page, rather than following a fixed two-part structure.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a complex or nuanced narrative and identify one clearly missing piece of information (e.g. "they never mention what the other person said") that suggests the account may be one-sided, in addition to summarizing events. Speaking: Can narrate a complex event fluently, integrating reported speech and shifting between what happened and its significance without a fixed template, adjusting register or pacing at least once in response to a specific listener reaction, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Told about a disagreement between two coworkers only from one person's account, the student notices and can point to the specific missing piece (the account never mentions what the other person actually said); retelling their own story about a project setback, the student notices the listener seems impatient and skips ahead to the outcome before circling back to one key detail that explains it.

Description: Can read an extended narrative and identify specific pacing choices as heightening or minimizing significance, separating stated events from clearly-signaled reactions, and locate at least one place where the narrative's tone visibly shifts partway through (e.g. from neutral to noticeably more sympathetic language).
Example: Given an account of a workplace incident that stays neutral until a final paragraph that turns notably more sympathetic to one person, the student identifies both the pacing choice that builds sympathy and locates exactly where the tone shifts to more sympathetic language.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated extended narrative that makes explicit why events mattered, shifting between narration and reflection without a fixed template, and adjusting register or approach at least once to address a specified reader's likely reaction, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Asked to recount a project that failed for an audience they know will be skeptical of excuses, the student narrates the failure plainly, then shifts to a more concrete, evidence-based register when explaining what they changed afterward, rather than following a fixed two-part structure.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a complex or technical explanation and evaluate the strength or limitation of the reasoning used. Speaking: Can explain a complex phenomenon fluently, integrating mechanism and likely misconceptions without a fixed template, adjusting depth or register at least once in response to a specific listener signal of confusion or familiarity, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Explaining why their internet is slow, the student covers the actual cause, adds unprompted that it's not the router like people usually think, then notices the listener already seems to know the basics and skips ahead to the more technical detail instead of re-explaining what's obvious.

Description: Can read an extended explanation and classify specific causal claims as direct cause or contributing factor, and locate at least one place where the explanation visibly shifts in technicality partway through (e.g. from plain language into denser vocabulary).
Example: Given an explanation of a product recall that starts in plain language and shifts into denser technical detail midway, the student classifies the causal claims as direct causes or contributing factors, and locates the point where the language shifts into denser technical vocabulary.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated extended explanation that distinguishes direct causes from contributing factors, shifting between accessible and technical register without a fixed template to serve a specified reader, and adjusting depth at least once to head off a likely point of confusion, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Asked to explain a recurring problem at work to a manager who isn't technical, the student separates the main cause from contributing factors, then adds a plain-language aside right where a non-technical reader would otherwise get lost, rather than following a fixed two-part structure.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a complex set of instructions for an unfamiliar procedure and evaluate its efficiency or appropriateness for the context. Speaking: Can give instructions for a complex procedure fluently, integrating conditional branching without a fixed template, adjusting detail or pacing at least once in response to a specific listener signal of confusion or confidence, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Explaining how to file an expense report, the student covers the standard steps, adds unprompted what to do if a receipt is missing, then notices the listener nodding along confidently and speeds through the remaining routine steps rather than over-explaining them.

Description: Can read an extended set of instructions and classify individual steps as essential, recommended, or optional, identifying specific language that signals each step's priority, and identifying at least one place where the level of detail shifts to match a step's risk or complexity.
Example: Given software setup instructions that stay brief until a step involving account security, where the language becomes noticeably more detailed and cautious, the student classifies the priority of each step and identifies that shift as the writer flagging higher risk.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated set of instructions that adapts explanation depth to anticipated user skill level, shifting detail without a fixed template to match each step's risk or complexity, and adjusting register at least once for a step most users get stuck on, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Asked to write setup instructions for a new team member, the student keeps most steps brief but adds noticeably more detail and a plainer tone at the exact step new hires usually get stuck on, rather than giving every step equal treatment.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended evaluation of something and evaluate the validity of the judgment made. Speaking: Can evaluate something fluently, integrating explicit, well-justified criteria and a verdict without a fixed template, adjusting emphasis or tone at least once in response to a specific listener pushback, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Evaluating a service they use, the student states their criteria, gives a verdict, adds unprompted that some people say it's overpriced but disagrees for what you get, then hears genuine pushback on that point and shifts to a more concrete example to defend it rather than repeating the same claim.

Description: Can read an extended evaluation and evaluate how the writer weighs criteria against one another to reach an overall judgment, distinguishing a justified conclusion from a merely asserted one, and locate at least one place where the writer's language visibly becomes more defensive or detailed (a likely response to pushback), without needing to infer the specific objection being addressed.
Example: Given a product review that stays measured until a paragraph that turns noticeably more detailed and defensive, the student identifies the writer's actual reasoning versus restated opinion, and locates the point where the writing becomes more defensive in tone.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated extended evaluation that weighs criteria against one another to reach a justified overall judgment, shifting tone without a fixed template to address a likely counter-evaluation, and adjusting emphasis at least once for a specified skeptical reader, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Asked to evaluate two commute options for a reader who's already said they hate long commutes, the student weighs time against cost, then gives extra weight and detail to the time comparison specifically because that's what the reader cares about most.

Description: Listening: Can listen to an extended argument and evaluate the strength of its evidence and reasoning. Speaking: Can construct a fluent, well-evidenced argument, integrating a rebutted counterargument without a fixed template, qualifying claims appropriately, and adjusting strategy or tone at least once in response to specific listener pushback, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Arguing for a change at work, the student presents the case, adds unprompted that it'll slow things down at first but pays off long-term, then hears real pushback on the short-term cost and shifts from asserting the long-term gain to citing a specific number to back it up.

Description: Can read an extended argument and evaluate how the writer weighs the strength of evidence against the counterargument to reach a qualified conclusion, distinguishing a well-supported conclusion from an overstated one, and locate at least one place where the writer's approach visibly shifts (e.g. from principle-based claims to concrete data), without needing to infer the specific objection being anticipated.
Example: Given an opinion piece that argues from principle early on and shifts to concrete data partway through, the student evaluates whether the conclusion is actually supported, and locates the point where the argument shifts from principle-based claims to data-based claims.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated extended argument that weighs its own evidence against a counterargument to reach a persuasive, qualified conclusion, shifting strategy without a fixed template, and adjusting tone at least once for a specified skeptical reader, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Asked their opinion on a workplace policy change for an audience they know is skeptical, the student presents their case, then shifts from a confident to a more measured, evidence-first tone specifically at the point where they address the main objection.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a complex or high-stakes transactional exchange and evaluate whether the approach taken was effective. Speaking: Can carry out a complex transactional exchange fluently, integrating persuasive and diplomatic language without a fixed template, and adjusting strategy or tone at least once in response to a specific reaction from the other party, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Disputing an incorrect charge, the student states the issue clearly and proposes a resolution, then notices the representative getting defensive, shifts to a more collaborative tone and reframes the request as a shared problem to solve rather than repeating the original complaint.

Description: Can read a transactional communication and identify the stated request, and locate at least one place where the writer's tone visibly shifts as the message progresses (e.g. from diplomatic to more direct), without needing to infer the writer's underlying strategy for that shift.
Example: Given a complaint email that opens diplomatically and grows more direct by the final paragraph, the student identifies the actual request stated in the opening, and locates the point where the writer's language becomes noticeably more direct.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated transactional message that adjusts tone and strategy for a sensitive situation, shifting register without a fixed template as the message progresses, and adjusting approach at least once for a specified likely reaction from the reader, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Writing a formal complaint about a service issue to a company known for slow responses, the student opens diplomatically, states the problem clearly, then shifts to more direct, specific language when requesting a resolution, anticipating the reader might otherwise not act on it.

Description: Listening: Can listen to a complex or delicate social exchange and evaluate whether the response given was socially appropriate. Speaking: Can navigate a complex social exchange fluently, integrating diplomatic and face-saving language without a fixed template, and adjusting tone or approach at least once in response to a specific reaction from the other person, using complex sentence structures with sustained control.
Example: Needing to correct a friend's misunderstanding without embarrassing them, the student does so gently, checks in on how they're taking it, notices the friend still seems hurt, and shifts to a warmer, more reassuring tone before moving the conversation forward.

Description: Can read a social communication and identify tactful phrasing versus a blunt statement of the same content, and locate at least one place where the writer's tone visibly shifts as the message progresses (e.g. from warm to more careful and formal), without needing to infer the writer's underlying emotional state.
Example: Given a message declining an invitation that opens warmly and grows more careful and formal toward the actual "no," the student identifies which phrases are softening the refusal, and locates the point where the message's tone becomes more careful and formal.

Description: Can write a fluent, integrated social message that navigates a socially delicate situation with sustained tact, shifting register without a fixed template as the message progresses, and adjusting tone at least once for a specified likely reaction from the reader, using complex sentence structures with sustained control and high independence.
Example: Writing to decline a friend's business proposal without damaging the friendship, the student opens warmly, softens the refusal itself, then shifts to a slightly more practical, reassuring tone toward the end anticipating the friend might worry about the friendship itself.

Description: Listening: Can listen to two extended spoken descriptions of the same subject, critically assess how each speaker's rhetorical choices shape a different impression, and identify at least one unstated interest or assumption behind one speaker's framing that neither speaker states outright. Speaking: Can deliver a well-structured spoken description that deliberately selects and emphasizes detail to shape listener perception, self-monitoring and smoothly repairing at least one imprecise word choice mid-delivery, using idiomatic vocabulary and flexible register control.
Example: Given two spoken descriptions of the same neighborhood — one from a real estate agent, one from a resident — the student explains that the agent emphasizes proximity to downtown while omitting noise, and infers the agent's unstated interest in closing a sale even though it's never said; describing their own hometown afterward, the student catches themselves calling a street "dangerous," softens it to "not the safest at night," and continues without losing momentum.

Description: Can read two extended descriptions of the same subject, critically assess how each writer's rhetorical choices shape a different impression, and identify at least one unstated interest or assumption behind one writer's framing that isn't explicitly acknowledged, using sophisticated inference and register awareness.
Example: Given a paid ad and an independent review of the same restaurant, the student identifies which details each writer chose to include or omit, and infers that the ad's cheerful tone serves an unstated commercial interest the text never admits to.

Description: Can write a nuanced, well-structured extended description that shapes reader perception through deliberate selection and emphasis of detail, embeds at least one unstated implication the reader must infer rather than being told directly, and shows evidence of unprompted self-revision for clarity and effect, using sophisticated cohesion, idiomatic and precise vocabulary, and flexible register control.
Example: Asked to write a tourism-brochure description of their city, the student deliberately emphasizes its charm and downplays its traffic — letting the omission itself imply something a careful reader would notice — then revises the draft on their own to sharpen that framing further.

Description: Listening: Can listen to two extended narratives covering the same or related events, critically assess how each storyteller's structural choices shape what the listener is meant to conclude, and identify at least one unstated motive behind one teller's version that isn't directly admitted. Speaking: Can narrate with rhetorical control, deliberately shaping structure and emphasis for a specific audience effect, self-monitoring and smoothly repairing at least one point where the sequence of events comes out unclear.
Example: Given two colleagues' accounts of the same office conflict, the student identifies that one account opens with the other person's mistake and omits their own, and infers the unstated motive of protecting their own reputation; telling their own story about a project delay, the student notices they've described two events out of order, briefly clarifies the sequence, and continues smoothly.

Description: Can read two extended narratives covering the same or related events, critically assess how each writer's structural choices shape what the reader is meant to conclude, and identify at least one unstated motive or interest behind one writer's structural choices, using sophisticated inference and register awareness.
Example: Given two news articles about the same event with different opening paragraphs, the student identifies which is structured to build sympathy for a specific party, and infers the unstated editorial interest that shapes that structuring choice.

Description: Can write a nuanced, well-structured extended narrative that shapes reader understanding of significance through deliberate pacing and selection of detail, embeds at least one implication about a character's or the narrator's own motive that the reader must infer, and shows evidence of unprompted self-revision, using sophisticated cohesion, idiomatic and precise vocabulary, and flexible register control.
Example: Asked to write about a difficult decision, the student deliberately withholds the outcome until the final sentence and lets a small, unexplained detail earlier in the story hint at their real motive without stating it, then revises the pacing on their own.

Description: Listening: Can listen to two competing explanations of the same phenomenon, critically assess the underlying assumptions each relies on, and identify at least one unstated limitation or gap in the stronger explanation itself. Speaking: Can explain complex phenomena with precision and rhetorical control, deliberately structuring the explanation step-by-step for a specified audience, self-monitoring and smoothly repairing at least one point where the explanation gets ahead of what the audience likely follows.
Example: Given two explanations for a company's sales drop, the student identifies the unstated assumption each depends on, judges one more defensible, but also notes an unstated limitation in that stronger explanation; explaining a process to a colleague, the student notices a confused look, backs up one step, fills the gap, and continues without losing the thread.

Description: Can read two competing explanations of the same phenomenon, critically assess the underlying assumptions each relies on, and identify at least one unstated limitation in the more defensible explanation, using sophisticated inference and register awareness.
Example: Given two articles explaining the same finding at different levels of certainty, the student identifies which one overstates its evidence, and also flags an unstated limitation in the more careful article's own methodology.

Description: Can write a nuanced, well-structured extended explanation that anticipates and addresses reader misunderstanding or an alternative account, explicitly acknowledges at least one limitation of its own explanation rather than presenting it as complete, and shows evidence of unprompted self-revision, using sophisticated cohesion, precise technical/abstract vocabulary, and flexible register control.
Example: Asked to explain a technical process to a non-expert, the student writes a draft, adds a brief note acknowledging where the explanation simplifies something true experts would qualify further, then revises to remove jargon a lay reader wouldn't know.

Description: Listening: Can listen to two competing sets of instructions for the same task, critically assess gaps or unstated assumptions in each, and identify at least one assumption about user expertise that neither instruction set states outright. Speaking: Can give instructions with precision and rhetorical control, deliberately sequencing and emphasizing critical steps for a specified audience, self-monitoring and smoothly correcting at least one step given out of the most useful order.
Example: Given two sets of instructions for assembling the same furniture, the student identifies that one skips a step that matters for stability, and notes both sets silently assume the user already knows how to use a specific tool; walking someone through a process aloud, the student realizes they gave step four before step three, calmly reorders it, and continues.

Description: Can read two competing sets of instructions for the same task, critically assess how each anticipates edge cases and varying user contexts, and identify at least one unstated assumption about the user both instruction sets share, using sophisticated inference and register awareness.
Example: Given two recipes for the same dish, the student identifies which one better anticipates a common mistake like overcooking, and notes both recipes silently assume access to a specific piece of equipment.

Description: Can write a nuanced, well-structured extended set of instructions that anticipates edge cases and varying user contexts, explicitly states at least one assumption it's making about the user rather than leaving it implicit, and shows evidence of unprompted self-revision, using sophisticated cohesion, precise technical vocabulary, and flexible register control.
Example: Asked to write instructions for a complex software setup, the student states upfront what prior knowledge the reader is assumed to have, then revises a draft after noticing a step assumes something beyond that stated baseline.

Description: Listening: Can listen to two expert-level evaluations of the same thing that apply different standards, critically assess what each counts as "good," and identify at least one unstated interest or bias shaping one evaluator's standard. Speaking: Can evaluate with precision and rhetorical control, deliberately selecting and framing criteria to persuade a specified audience, self-monitoring and smoothly clarifying at least one criterion that comes across as vaguer than intended.
Example: Given two laptop reviews, the student identifies each reviewer's standard for "good" and infers that one reviewer's harsh take on price is likely shaped by writing for a budget-focused audience, not stated outright; evaluating a service aloud, the student notices their own criterion ("good value") sounded vague, clarifies what they actually mean, and continues.

Description: Can read two expert-level evaluations of the same thing that apply different standards, critically assess which is more defensible for a stated purpose, and identify at least one unstated interest shaping one evaluator's chosen standard, using sophisticated inference and register awareness.
Example: Given two restaurant reviews with opposite verdicts, the student identifies what each reviewer values most, and infers that one reviewer's harshness likely reflects an unstated expectation of fine-dining standards applied to a casual restaurant.

Description: Can write a nuanced, well-structured extended evaluation that questions or refines its own criteria, explicitly names the standard it's applying rather than leaving it implicit, and shows evidence of unprompted self-revision, using sophisticated cohesion, precise evaluative/critical vocabulary, and flexible register control.
Example: Asked to evaluate a service, the student states the standard they're judging by up front, then revises a draft after realizing the first version didn't clearly justify that standard.

Description: Listening: Can listen to two opposing expert-level arguments on the same issue, critically assess the logic of each, and identify at least one unstated premise either side is relying on without defending it. Speaking: Can construct an argument with precision and rhetorical control, deliberately sequencing claims and evidence for a specified audience, self-monitoring and smoothly strengthening at least one claim that comes across as weaker than intended once stated aloud.
Example: Given arguments for and against remote work, the student identifies a logical gap in one side's reasoning and also names an unstated premise the stronger side never defends; arguing a position aloud, the student hears their own claim land weakly, immediately adds a concrete example to back it up, and continues.

Description: Can read two opposing extended arguments on the same issue, critically assess the strength of each side's logic and evidence, and identify at least one unstated premise underlying the stronger argument, using sophisticated inference and register awareness.
Example: Given two opinion pieces on opposite sides of a policy debate, the student identifies which article's evidence is stronger, and also names an unstated premise that article relies on without ever defending it directly.

Description: Can write a nuanced, well-structured extended argument that anticipates multiple counterarguments and refutes or concedes them strategically, explicitly surfaces at least one premise its own argument depends on rather than leaving it assumed, and shows evidence of unprompted self-revision, using sophisticated cohesion, precise argumentative/rhetorical vocabulary, and flexible register control.
Example: Asked to argue a position, the student states plainly the underlying premise their argument depends on, then revises a draft after noticing they hadn't addressed the strongest counterargument.

Description: Listening: Can listen to both parties' accounts of the same high-stakes transactional exchange, critically assess the strategies each used, and identify at least one unstated goal behind one party's approach that they never state directly. Speaking: Can carry out a transactional exchange with precision and rhetorical control, deliberately selecting strategy for a specified outcome, self-monitoring and smoothly softening at least one phrasing that comes across as more forceful than intended.
